Pat Nevin sees a lot of Newcastle United.

The former Chelsea and Everton winger a regular visitor at St James’ Park.

Pat Nevin often on media duties at United matches.

As a result of that, he has far more of a clue than your average pundit about Newcastle United, the good an the bad.

The one-time player was once again on media duties at St James’ Park on Saturday night for the Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2 match.

As is usually a case, his reaction to what he witnessed was pretty spot on.

Pat Nevin on BBC Radio Five Live, commenting on the first half moment when Bruno Guimaraes almost headed Arsenal into the lead: “That would have broken a few hearts around here, a great run from Bruno Guimaraes. A very deep header, he’s a deep-lying midfielder. These Newcastle fans have watched him so many times in black and white and that was a decent half-chance.”

Pat Nevin after Eze gave Arsenal a 33rd minute lead: “You felt as though it was coming. The Newcastle midfielders pushed up further and the second they did so, they were shredded. That pass from Kai Havertz is an absolute delight, he’s such a special player. Eberechi Eze lashed it past goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek.”

Pat Nevin commenting after Harvey Barnes equalised four minutes after the break: “Newcastle have been fabulous at the start of the second half. They’ve closed down higher up the field, not giving Arsenal any time on the ball. They’ve struggled to be able to zip the ball about like they did in the first. But can Newcastle keep this up?”

Malick Thiaw giving United a 2-1 lead, Pat Nevin: “Beyond amazing. There is not a Newcastle fan in this ground who could see this coming. Pat Nevin as the match moves into the nine minutes of added time and the score 2-2, Noni Madueke having equalised on 78 minutes: “This has got the feeling of a cup tie. I love that Newcastle don’t want to settle just for a point against the champions. But I think they’re running out of players, Lewis Hall has sat down.”

Pat Nevin with a perfect summing up after the final whistle: “Isn’t it a joy when you think you know what’s going on in football but you know nothing at half-time. In the first half Arsenal were all over Newcastle, there was not one area where Arsenal were not better. Then three changes at half time and Newcastle were superb in the second half and the fans will be wondering where that has been all season? A great performance coming back after being a goal down. They showed the capabilities they’ve got.”

#2045. Scott Parker tells us there are positives – but talk is cheap | West Ham News

West Ham failed to overcome bottom side Preston North End in what was a desperately disappointing spectacle for West Ham fans who had been expecting so much more from their new manager’s first home game.

A scrappy first goal conceded came from pretty much Preston’s only attempt at goal, and then our visitors sat back in time-honoured tradition.  Four times the Hammers crashed the ball against the woodwork in a first half which showed plenty of promise, however the second half evaporated in familiar fashion, inexplicably, no sooner than Mavropanos crashed in the equaliser.

Just about every fan expected West Ham to go on and win the game convincingly – yet instead they huffed and puffed with endless ‘after you – no after you’ short, sideways passes as nobody took responsibility for making the killer pass or – heaven forbid- taking on the shot.

However, the West Ham manager will no doubt do his best, tomorrow maybe, to pull out positives, despite being ‘devastated‘ at the result:

Edson Álvarez, in his first game this season, El Machin was, surprisingly, up to speed pretty much immediately, sitting in front of the defence. He was everywhere: collecting, tidying up, harrying, attacking and breaking down opponents’ attacks. The late-tackling liability of last season was nowhere to be seen as he impressed and looks as if he has found himself a role for the coming weeks.

However, there’s a caveat: Remember this is the bottom side in the division who have just held us to draw. It will be intriguing to see if he copes against tougher opponents.

Edson Alvarez -Looked in control this afternoon – of his own discipline and of his midfield patch.

Finn Herrick: It can only have been unsettling, as the young keeper came to punch his first corner only to find a team mate’s glancing header got there first, looping the ball over his outstretched fists and allowing Preston to open the scoring against the run of play.

Credit to him, Herrick kept his cool and grew in stature as the game went on. He made an excellent double save after Mayers’ poor defensive header, and played well with the ball at his feet, combining Areola’s shot-stopping ability and Hermansen’s football skills.

However, positives aside, Parker has his work cut out simply to get this team’s work rate up. This time, they started quick and could have had three in the first half, even though there was a hesitancy and a lack of creation in front of goal.

Why it evaporated no sooner than the Hammers had equalised was a mystery. What should have become a barrage launched on Preston’s goal became a last thirty minutes of frustrating misfiring.

Just. Not. Good.Enough. Despite the bright points which Parker referenced in his post – match conference.

Just don’t blame West Ham’s newest manager for the failure of the last three to demand pacy, attacking football and recruiting so-called strikers who wouldn’t have made it into West Ham’s championships side of 2004/5 or 2011/12.

Can’t make a silk purse out of a sows ear. Especially not in two weeks.

#2044. Stark reality of Sporting Director transfer dealings laid bare in front of Yasir Al-Rumayyan

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

It was well-publicised ahead of the match that Yasir Al-Rumayyan would be at St James’ Park for the Newcastle United match against Arsenal.

A chance for the Newcastle United Chairman to see for himself at close quarters how things are now looking.

Yasir Al-Rumayyan seeing a game of two halves.

Newcastle United struggling to get out of their own half in the opening 45 minutes as Arsenal dominated and led 1-0 at the break.

Matthias Jaissle making three substitutions at the break and a totally different Newcastle United on show, by far the better team that ‘won’ the second half 2-1.

By the final whistle, Newcastle United had certainaly deserved at least a point, possibly all three.

The brilliant second half comeback was achieved due to the following 13 Newcastle United players and these 13 can be separated as follows:

Already at St James’ Park pre-Eddie Howe:

Tino Livramento, Malick Thiaw, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall, Sven Botman, Jacob Ramsey, Harvey Barnes, Yoane Wissa, Anthony Elanga, William Osula

Ahead of summer 2026, Newcastle United Chairman Yasir Al-Rumayyan took control of transfers from Eddie Howe and gave it to Ross Wilson.

Eddie Howe (and then Matthias Jaissle) still having some say but Ross Wilson the one dictating the overall transfer policy and holding the power.

This isn’t unusual, many clubs having a similar strategy of handing the Sporting Director control of transfer policy.

Ross Wilson the key man this summer in deciding to sell Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes, as well as not renewing the contracts of Kieran Trippier and a number of other older players.

Altogether, approximately £260m/£270m was committed on new signings by Ross Wilson to rebuild the Newcastle United team and squad. Yasir Al-Rumayyan must have been wondering where they all were in that second half against Arsenal…

Amar Dedic – Subbed off after playing the first 45 minutes against Arsenal Sean Steur – Subbed off after playing the first 45 minutes against Arsenal Nico Gonzalez – An unused sub Matias Fernandez-Pardo – An unused sub Bazoumana Toure – Left out of the matchday squad Aladji Bamba – Left out of the matchday squad Ewen Jaouen – Injured Ousmane Diabate – On loan for the season at Turkish top tier club Gençlerbirliği

It is still early days and we need a lot longer to judge properly when it comes to allowing Ross Wilson control of transfers in and out.

However, there are inherent weaknesses with a system whereby the Sporting Director and not the Manager/Head Coach has control of selecting which players are signed and which are sold/let go.

As things stand, Matthias Jaissle clearly overwhelmingly feels he has to rely at this moment in time on players who came in before Ross Wilson’s summer of 2026. Players who have been at the club for some time, less star players such as Gordon, Tonali, Trippier and Bruno who the Sporting Director wanted/agreed to move on this summer.

By the end of this season we should have a better idea about his signings.

I certainly don’t think it is a total disaster, at least not longer-term. I think already I have seen enough of the likes of Hornicek, Steur and Dedic to believe that they are decent additions. I think Fernandez-Pardi will work out and I believe Nico Gonzalez will be okay. With the others they clearly need more time before we can judge them at all.

However, you don’t always get to tomorrow, if you can’t get through today…

For me it is very clear that Matthias Jaissle has walked into a situation where he has been left well short by Ross Wilson of a fully stocked and prepared squad to take on this 2026-27 season.

A case of needing to battle through this campaign and then hopefully as a group the summer 2026 signings can grow and help Newcastle United evolve. In the meantime, it is the established old guard that Matthias Jaissle will clearly need to have the main focus on.

#2043. West Ham 1-1 Preston: Scott Parker Still Struggling To Unlock Jarrod Bowen

West Ham were nowhere near good enough against the worst team in the division. Whilst we had our chances, it would be a long stretch to suggest we were significantly better than Preston, particularly during a first half in which the visitors created opportunities of their own.

Edson Álvarez looked decent enough on his return to the team, but Scott Parker looks no closer to getting the best out of Jarrod Bowen than Nuno Espírito Santo or Graham Potter did. In essence, the Hammers lacked magic, and watching our best player pinned to the right flank was depressing.

The statistics certainly make for interesting reading. West Ham registered 30 attempts on goal, but only four were on target. We also hit the woodwork three times, with Bowen and Joël Veltman striking opposite posts during the same passage of play before Edvin Austbø rattled the crossbar shortly after half-time.

Preston took the lead through Liam Lindsay after just 18 minutes, following a corner which Joël Piroe inadvertently flicked towards his own goal.

Konstantinos Mavropanos eventually equalised on the hour mark, heading home Arne Engels’ cross after Manor Solomon had helped create the opening.

Yet even after drawing level, West Ham couldn’t find a winner against a team who arrived at the London Stadium bottom of the Championship.

There were chances, certainly. Tomáš Souček had a late header tipped over, while Mavropanos headed over in stoppage time. But for all the possession and pressure, there was precious little composure in front of goal.

And as far as I’m concerned, this was a match West Ham simply had to win.

What makes the situation particularly frustrating is that we’ve already seen what Bowen can do when he’s given more freedom.

During the remarkable comeback against Cardiff City, our captain was allowed to drift into central positions, where he caused all sorts of problems. His movement, passing and ability to find space helped transform a game which had looked completely lost at half-time.

I was so impressed that I subsequently wrote about how Scott Parker needed to restore West Ham’s most dangerous weapon.

Unfortunately, against Blackburn, Bowen was back operating as a conventional right winger. And against Preston, we saw much the same thing.

That’s not to suggest Bowen didn’t contribute. He was involved throughout and managed eight attempts on goal, including the effort which struck the post.

But there’s a difference between getting Bowen involved in the game and getting the best out of him.

West Ham have spent far too long relying on our captain to produce something special from wide positions, often with defenders able to anticipate where he’s going to receive the ball.

Against Cardiff, we briefly saw something different.

Bowen was the inspiration behind that second-half recovery. He looked far more dangerous when he was able to move into the middle and influence the game rather than remaining tied to the touchline.

I genuinely thought Parker had stumbled upon something which could change West Ham’s season.

Instead, two matches later, we seem to have gone backwards.

Of course, the manager has plenty of other issues demanding his attention.

There were some positives against Preston. Álvarez made his first Championship appearance for West Ham since May 2025 and looked reasonably comfortable in midfield, while young goalkeeper Finlay Herrick produced an excellent double save to prevent the visitors doubling their lead.

Mavropanos also deserves credit for another important goal, particularly given that he is a centre-back who continues to contribute at the other end of the pitch.

But the bigger picture remains deeply concerning.

West Ham simply had to start turning the London Stadium into somewhere opposition teams feared visiting.

Instead, the bottom club have come away with a point, and Parker has now overseen two draws and a defeat in his first three matches.

I appreciate he hasn’t been in the job long, and I’m not suggesting he’s solely responsible for problems which have been developing for some considerable time.

However, the international break gave him an opportunity to work with the players, and I had hoped to see considerably more improvement than we witnessed.

For me, the biggest concern remains our inability to get the best out of Bowen.

We have a player capable of providing the creativity, movement and unpredictability that this team so desperately needs. Yet we’re still asking him to spend most of his time playing in the same predictable areas of the pitch.

West Ham don’t lack effort. Against Preston, they certainly didn’t lack possession or attempts on goal.

And until Scott Parker finds a way of giving Jarrod Bowen the freedom to provide it, I fear we’re going to see plenty more afternoons like this one.

#2042. Expected Goals stats tell the very real story after Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Expected Goals is widely agreed to be the best way of measuring how well Premier League clubs play in any particular game.

To get a better look at how sides are doing, the Expected Goals (xG) metric allows you to get a better picture of just how teams are performing.

Expected goals (xG) is a statistic used to work out how many goals should be scored in a match.

With every single shot awarded an xG value based on the difficulty of the attempt, with factors including distance from goal, type of shot and number of defenders present affecting the value.

The higher the xG of a particular shot, the more likely a goal should be scored from that shot.

The xG value of every shot in a game is then used to calculate the expected goals in a particular match.

So rather than just the usual basic statistics of how many shots each team has, Expected Goals factors in where shots were taken from and how good a chance was and whether defenders in the way etc.

These Expected Goals stats from Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2

As you can see, Newcastle’s Expected Goals stat is higher than Arsenal’s by a decent degree. Not a huge difference but a clear one.

When you look at the other stats below, they back up the fact that Newcastle United deserved at the very least a point AND arguably if either side deserved to have won the game, it was United, as they had the better chances overall.

As well as the higher Expected Goals stat, Newcastle had twice as many corners (6 v 3), whilst the overall shots (12 v 13) and efforts on target (3 v 4) were almost identical.

We asked Davey Hat-Trick to give us his match ratings and player comments after Newcastle 2 Arsenal 2 in the Premier League.

Out of the 1,000+ games I have watched in person, the 4-4 draw with Arsenal 15 years ago is the match that most deserves the ‘game of two halves’ label. This one – against the same opponents – wasn’t far off.

A blind man could have seen the gulf in class between the two sides in the first half. Arsenal outclassed Newcastle without trying. Newcastle looked petrified, and it looked like no one wanted the ball. Having said that, Arsenal only scored a single goal, and didn’t really come that close again. Our centre halves were good.

The second half could not have been more different. Newcastle tore into Arsenal from the get-go, and the Gunners looked shell-shocked. By the time Arsenal had recovered their composure, Newcastle were 2-1 up. In my opinion, we were playing as well as we had all season.

Arsenal were bound to come back into it, and they did. They scored an equaliser, but that’s not to say Newcastle were overwhelmed. We were giving as good as we got, and continued to do so.

Having conceded, most Geordies were fearing the traditional last-minute winner for our opponents, and when the officials came up with nine minutes of injury time, it seemed nailed on.

But Newcastle held firm, and got a deserved point against the reigning champions, and this season’s most likely winners. It was a triumph of belief, effort, teamwork and quality, and it had a galvanising effect on the black and white faithful. St James’ Park was rocking to a degree I haven’t witnessed since our opener against Liverpool.

It’s hard to give the players a sensible mark. Everyone was poor in the first half. Everyone was excellent in the second.

Lukáš Horníček 5 Not at fault for Arsenal’s first, may have done better for their second, but he always looked nervy and unsure with the ball at his feet. His distribution was poor and he never looked confident.

Amar Dedić 4 Good player, bad game. Stranded for Arsenal’s first and took a pointless yellow card way before half time. Subbed off at half time, a bold move by the manager, but the correct one.

Malick Thiaw 8 If it wasn’t for our centre halves, Arsenal could have been 3-0 up at half time. Their challenges, blocks and clearances kept Newcastle in the game. Just. The second half saw Thiaw liberated to pick his passes, get up the pitch and score Newcastle’s second from all of four inches.

Dan Burn 8 A captain’s innings. Kept the Gunners from tearing us apart in the first half and made a nuisance of himself in attack in the second. I thought he wouldn’t get much game time this campaign. Now he’s one of the first names on the team sheet.

Lewis Hall 6 People – me included – were calling him the best left back in the world this week. I still think he is…but he wasn’t anything like that in that first half. Was mugged for Arsenal’s first and made a few other errors. He typified Newcastle’s second half – a much improved performance. Got up the pitch and had Arsenal on the back foot. Went off with what looked like a strain. Let’s hope it’s nothing serious.

Sean Steur 5 The game passed him by in the first half and he didn’t appear for the second. I don’t think he was bad, just not particularly effective.

Lewis Miley 6 A mate of mine thinks he was our best player. I just thought it was a decent game from Lewis. Not exactly dominant, but decent on the ball, and another wiho improved in the second half. Had a run at goal which nearly came off.

Jacob Murphy 5 I only remember Newcastle having one attempt in the first half and it was Murphy who had it. It was on target as well, except it hit his own team-mate. Other than that, Jacob offered little else and was hooked at half time.

Joe Willock 6 He’d be on a 7 or 8 if he got his head up and passed the ball instead of taking on ridiculous long distance shots. I thought he had a decent game, to be fair, and was full of energy. It looked to me like he played deeper in the second half and it worked. I think he got a dodgy assist for Thiaw’s goal.

Harvey Barnes 8 Another who seemed like a bystander in the first half but who came to life in the second. Scored the goal that gave us belief and even went past his man a few times on the wing. Well played lad.

William Osula 6.5 There will be some who say Osula ‘did nowt’ in the first half but I think that was due to his team-mates being pinned back in their own half. He was isolated, although he showed his usual willingness to run. Second half was a different game. His colleagues actually got up the pitch to support him and he looked much better. A good assist for our first goal and it became a more confident display.

Tino Livramento 7 I’d forgotten what an excellent footballer Tino can be. He came on for the second half and looked like the player we saw two seasons ago. Quick, intelligent and good on the ball. It’s fair to say the half-time substitutes improved the team; none more than Tino.

Anthony Elanga 5.5 To be truthful, he didn’t do a lot with the ball that I remember, but he did inject pace and energy, qualities that were non-existent first half. We looked a different team. We were a different team.

Jacob Ramsey 6 We looked more secure when Jacob entered the fray. Suddenly our midfield looked better than Arsenal’s. Played some good balls but skied a shot that could have won us the game.

Yoane Wissa 4 On for a tiring Willock. Found it difficult to get into the game.

Sven Botman 5 Came on at a time when most fans’ hearts were in their mouths – Arsenal were looking dangerous. But Sven held his own and looked the part. Relief all round.

#2039. West Ham 1 – 1 Preston North End : The morning after

That eight point gap between West Ham United in tenth and the Championship front runners is starting to look mighty huge with just sixteen games completed.

Of course the reality is that there are still thirty games remaining but West Ham will have to find a way of converting all the huffing and puffing into points or else we will find ourselves scratching around even trying to make the enlarged play off places come May next year.

“Wasteful West Ham”: Not my words but the description on the official club web site which sums up perfectly an afternoon of toil and frustration against the bottom side in the league.

Scott Parker pronounced himself happy with the effort, if ‘bitterly disappointed’ with the result. As were we all.

The team announcement produced a wave of optimism, and I’m not sure yet that we should ditch that: Tenth place is not where we expected to be at the end of November but there is still plenty of time to turn the West Ham supertanker back on course and away from the rocky peril of mid table, second division mediocrity.

But three years’ decline won’t be fixed in three games.

Introducing Fin Herrick and Edson Alvarez were bold decisions which could have backfired totally, especially after the maddening concession in the first half. Now Scott Parker needs to keep his nerve and persevere with that set up, go again on Tuesday night away at Fratton Park and trust for better luck and better finishing.

Ninety points still up for grabs this season, Hammers.

At least the ownership saw fit to ditch Nuno in time to turn the ship around. In the bad old days of David Sullivan, we’d still be on about game 5 of 20 ‘must win’ games before Nuno had to walk the plank. (Not sure where all the nautical terms came from this morning).

In any case, there’s not another manager who’d do any better in Scott Parker’s place right now. Don’t panic. Yet. COYI!

#2038. GdS: ‘The Italian option’ – Milan also considering move for ‘blossoming’ Calvani

AC Milan could launch a bid to sign Gabriele Calvani next year, with the young Italian coming into his own in Serie A.

Whilst Milan are becoming more comfortable with buying experienced options, Gerry Cardinale will not abandon the future. So, they’ll continue to try to buy the right players for the future where the opportunity to do so is right; for example, with Sankhoun Diawara.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Gazzetta dello Sport states that Goncalo Inacio is an ‘of course’ option, whilst Virgil van Dijk sits as a ‘why not’. For Calvani, though, the reasoning is more in-depth. He’s not up to the level of his European counterparts just yet, but a promising Italian is something in its own right.

He’s blossomed this year with Frosinone, playing on the right in a 4-2-3-1 set-up. So, there’d be a potential spot for him to replace Fikayo Tomori if he were to depart next year. However, they’d have to deal with Genoa, who are his parent club.

Now could be the perfect time to introduce him to San Siro, allowing him to develop in his own time without needing to push him. For his first season in Serie A, he’s taking to it brilliantly from his pressing to his aerial ability.

They’ll hope to be able to watch him at San Siro this weekend, but it’s tough to know if they’ll be able to, given he’s struggling with a flexor issue currently. Nevertheless, he’s a concrete target; practical and with potential for the future.

#2037. And so it came to pass with Bruno Guimaraes… Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The reaction to the departure of Bruno Guimaraes seems to have overshadowed that of Alexander Isak.

Fans had assumed the Brazilian’s deep connection with the United faithful was mutual, so discovering it was a bit more one-sided than anyone believed, only heightened the sense of betrayal when he left for the Emirates

Some writers on The Mag were asked for 50 words on Bruno Guimaraes ahead of this match; most accepting that he’s still a legend, but that the manner of his departure left a sour taste such that he shouldn’t have been immune to a tempestuous reception.

And so it came to pass; Guimaraes was roundly booed and jeered, with both his greed and his parentage loudly called into question, which felt a touch ironic, given how the faithful had once adored his father, a man who used to sit in the away end and soak up the adulation.

As it happens, Bruno was largely anonymous and replaced by the more energetic Lewis-Skelly when his side was trailing, although he hadn’t been far from converting a Declan Rice cross in the 28th minute, something that would have amounted to a low blow for most of the 52,661 crowd had his effort found its way into the back of the net.

That chance came just before Arsenal’s dominance saw them ahead. Kai Havertz dispossessed Lewis Hall high up the pitch and slid a sublime pass to Eberechi Eze, who whipped the ball past Lukas Hornicek.

Newcastle were struggling and it was what I’d expected, pre-match bonhomie with old friends and the lad, fueled by some decent ale, had quickly evaporated when the team was announced.

Right on half-time, Madueke, who had already hit the base of the post in the sixth minute, passed up a golden opportunity to double Arsenal’s lead, as some of the boos that had been reserved for Bruno were now being directed at those in the black and white.

Thank goodness Matthias Jaissle had both seen enough and managed to hold his nerve, a decisive triple substitution that introduced Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey, and Anthony Elanga into the fray proving transformational.

Just four minutes after the restart, Joe Willock pressed Martin Odegaard into a costly mistake on the Arsenal left. Will Osula scooped up the loose ball and teed up Harvey Barnes, who fired clinically past David Raya to register United’s first home strike in over two months.

Barnes will tear you apart echoed around the stadium, Dedic unable to join in with the bow and arrow celebrations, Livramento now doing a better job at right back, whilst Ramsey had shored up the midfield as Steur’s replacement and Elanga looked a whole lot better than the lethargic Murphy.

Energised by a crowd that was itself suitably invigorated, United turned the game on its head.

In the 62nd minute, Lewis Hall’s corner was nodded back across goal by an unmarked Dan Burn. This sparked a frenetic goalmouth scramble that ended with Malick Thiaw poking home from close range, a goal confirmed after an agonising VAR check that looked at supposed handball and offside offences, that feeling of dread never materialising as Chris Kavanagh finally signalled the goal would stand.

At this stage, United were very much on top but just couldn’t muster that elusive third, and when David Raya left the field following a collision with Osula in the 70th minute, rather than worsen the Gunners evening, the long break before Kepa Arrizabalaga replaced his compatriot allowed them to regroup and turn the tide.

I’d said to the lad that this was going to be a long twenty minutes, possibly half an hour, for us to negotiate and somewhat inevitably, Arsenal hit us on the counter in the 78th minute.

Released down the flank by Odegaard, Noni Madueke cut inside to drill a shot that squirmed through Hornicek’s grasp to level the scores. Could he have saved it? Maybe, all that good work at Craven Cottage a fortnight ago undone in an instant.

At this point, had anyone feared an Arsenal winner was coming, that might have been justified, they are a very good team and their substitutions demonstrated a squad that has strength in depth.

But the final stages, including nine minutes of added time, saw both sides pushing for a winner and it’s Newcastle that will feel more aggrieved, first Kepa denied Lewis Miley before Havertz nearly scored an own goal, the crossbar coming to his rescue as the spoils were shared.

I wrote an article for The Mag recently highlighting that United had picked up five more points from their opening ten fixtures when making a comparison with the same fixtures from the previous campaign. You can make that six following yesterday’s gutsy performance, and you never know, Matty Jaissle might just be getting the hang of things in the St James’ hotseat.

Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2 – Saturday 21 November 2026 5.30pm

Shots on target were Newcastle 3 Arsenal 4

Touches in the opposition box Newcastle 15 Arsenal 24

Hornicek, Dedic (Livramento 46), Thiaw, Burn, Hall (Botman 92), Miley, Steur (Ramsey 46), Barnes, Willock (Wissa 83), Murphy (Elanga 46), Osula

#2036. Two more points lost but Scott Parker’s gamble paid off | West Ham News

Just over one year ago, West Ham’s Finlay Herrick was stepping out on loan for Boreham Wood in the National League – the fifth tier of English football. A far cry from London Stadium yesterday as he replaced Mads Hermansen in goal and made his Championship debut, apparently hearing about his impending start just on the morning of the game.

And despite the first half concession from the corner, Herrick did a pretty fair job with excellent double saves later in the game and some assured glove work catching the ball – which had seemed like a lost art at times in the last couple of years.

Herrick after his unforgettable FA Cup penalty shootout debut last year

This was a massive gamble by Scott Parker which could have backfired dreadfully. With no Areola, the temptation must have been to revert to Hermansen yet the Hammers’ head coach stuck with his instinct. After the first half goal concession, Parker must have wondered – briefly – whether he’d made a huge howler.

Has Herrick done enough to keep his place? It seems Parker is dead set on replacing Hermansen so until Alphonse Areola is ‘fit and ready’ then Herrick should be prepared for more pitch time. He certainly has the ambition:

“I hope this is the start. I hope I’ve done myself justice and proved to the fans that I don’t just want to be third choice, I want to be playing, I want to get back to the Premier League and be part of that”. (whu/youtube)

Describing the competition amongst the trio of goal keepers, Herrick was quick to praise Hermansen for the encouragement and help he’s received recently, describing the three keepers as a team more than individuals fighting amongst themselves for the sole starting spot:

“There’s one goal keeper shirt and there’s three of us – but we’re like a band of brothers and we always stick together, me Mads and Fonz- no matter what. “

Difficult to believe Herrick is still only 20 – he seems to have been around West Ham’s fringes for ever- but he joined the academy at six years old and looks to have the talent to go all the way. From yesterday’s solid start, he didn’t let his manager or his team mates down and should feel rightly pretty proud of himself.

The question for Scott Parker is whether he continues between the sticks at Fratton Park on Tuesday night.

#2035. Newcastle United set new attendance record at St James’ Park

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

An increase to the St James’ Park capacity was officially announced by Newcastle United, this news came on the Friday (21 August 2026) afternoon ahead of the Liverpool match.

The Newcastle United owners announcing the St James’ Park increased capacity as part of a number of improvements (see below).

The official announcement stating: ‘We’ve expanded our safe standing provision with the introduction of new safe standing areas on Level 7. Thanks to additional work carried out by our operations team, we’ve also increased stadium capacity by approximately 500 seats, taking St. James’ Park’s capacity to 52,719 – enabling more supporters to experience live football in person.’

Obviously not the tens of thousands increase in stadium capacity that we are all waiting to hear about BUT every little helps. Up to another 500 Newcastle United fans extra able to get into each St James’ Park match.

For the Liverpool match it was a new Premier League era home record attendance for Newcastle United, a crowd of 52,630.

That St James’ Park record in the Premier League era was then broken again when 52,643 was the official attendance for the Bournemouth game on 5 September.

Then on September 19 against Hull City, the PL era record at SJP broken yet again, with 52,647 inside St James’ Park.

Now on Saturday 21 November for the 2-2 draw with Arsenal, edging up to 52,661.

That 21 August 2026 announcement also included: ‘We’ve invested £10 million into our hospitality offering, delivering one of the most extensive upgrade programmes ever undertaken at St. James’ Park. Highlights include full refurbishments of the Chairman’s Suite, and transformation of The Magpie into a stunning new pitch view hospitality space, Tidings. Plus, we’ve reimagined Heroes into Icons, which is a tribute to Newcastle United legends and inspired by one of the club’s most iconic retro kits. Additional improvements have been made across the Barracks, Four Corners and Moncur Suites, alongside the transformation of 22 executive boxes.’

The St James’ Park pitch also having money spent on it: ‘This summer has also seen a significant investment in the heart of the stadium, with £3.6 million invested in a brand-new pitch structure; the first complete replacement in 21 years. The project includes the installation of a state-of-the-art SubAir system, helping to maintain playing conditions throughout the season.’

The club also detailing: ‘Over the summer, we’ve completed a stadium-wide PA system upgrade and invested £2 million in a new LED floodlighting system, complete with a backup generator to improve resilience.

Work has also continued on improving mobile connectivity through the rollout of full stadium 5G infrastructure, helping supporters stay connected on matchdays. We’ve also installed four new in‑bowl replay screens, enhancing visibility of replays and key moments during games for supporters across the stadium.’

#2034. Call Me Crazy, But I’m Still Backing This West Ham Team – Here’s Why

As I left the London Stadium to a chorus of boos, I found myself desperately searching for positives from a frustrating 1-1 draw against the league’s bottom club.

The first was the performance of Alvarez. Largely cast into the shadows through the stubbornness of our former manager, he grabbed the game by the scruff of the neck. He took control, lifted the crowd, and, above all, displayed the leadership qualities this team has lacked for much of the season.

The second positive was that the statistics backed up what I’d watched unfold on the pitch. West Ham dominated possession with 79%, registered 30 shots, and recorded an xG of 3.13. The problem? Only four of those efforts were shots on target.

We gifted Preston their opening goal. It came from a calamitous mix-up, with Piroe’s flicked header looping backwards onto the crossbar before dropping kindly for Liam Lindsay to tap home from close range. It could be argued that Herrick should have been more commanding from the corner, but he made amends later with an excellent double save.

There were concerns that we wouldn’t pull one back, we did on the 60th minute, Mavropanos heading home his sixth goal in 15 league appearances this season.

“Ifs” and “buts” don’t win football matches, and as Parker said afterwards: “The overall performance suggests we should win. The fine margins of football are, and the reality is, if Tomas Soucek scores that last-minute goal, it’s probably a different interview.”

For me, I’m not going to be negative. We needed a win and we didn’t get the three points, but what I want to see now is the team build on the domination, the chance creation and the shot volume by going to Fratton Park on Tuesday and getting the job done. If we concede first there and deliver an abject performance, then and only then will there be more serious questions to ask.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

If the ball falls to a Newcastle United player in the penalty area, who do you want that player to be?

Harvey Barnes is such a natural finisher, one of the very best.

His strike against Arsenal on Saturday night was his 100th career goal.

However, when you drill down, his Premier League direct goal contributions (scoring and assisting) are even better than that bare stat of a century of career goals.

Down below I have detailed the Harvey Barnes Premier League record these last seven and a bit seasons.

From the start of the 2019/20 Premier League season onwards, the first four for Leicester and then three and a bit for NUFC.

My only surprise is how surprised so many people are, at just how good and productive Harvey Barnes has been across so many seasons.

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 149 minutes

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 150 minutes

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 131 minutes

14 Direct Goal involvements (13 goals and 1 assist) – 2,720 PL minutes played

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 194 minutes

2023/24 Premier League (Newcastle United)

8 Direct Goal involvements (5 goals and 3 assists) – 795 PL minutes played

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 99 minutes

2024/25 Premier League (Newcastle United)

13 Direct Goal involvements (9 goals and 4 assists) – 1,756 PL minutes played

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 135 minutes

2025/26 Premier League (Newcastle United)

8 Direct Goal involvements (7 goals and 1 assist) – 1,964PL minutes played

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 245 minutes

2026/27 Premier League (Newcastle United)

5 Direct Goal involvements (3 goals and 2 assists) – 977 PL minutes played

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 195 minutes

Total Harvey Barnes Direct Goal involvements these past seven and a bit Premier League seasons (for Leicester and Newcastle):

91 Direct Goal involvements (58 goals and 33 assists) – 14,363 PL minutes played

A Harvey Barnes direct goal involvement once every 157 Premier League minutes, from the start of the 2019/20 PL season onwards across seven and a bit Premier League seasons.

This season for Newcastle United, Harvey Barnes has scored or assisted a third (five) of United’s 15 Premier League goals. Whilst if you add his two Carabao Cup goals, that makes it seven direct goal involvements already in all competitions this season, scoring five and two assists.

#2032. CM: How much Hutchinson’s ‘dream’ permanent move to Milan would cost

In the summer, AC Milan included a buy option in the loan deal to bring Omari Hutchinson to San Siro, but what would be the cost?

Speaking in recent days, Hutchinson has admitted that a move to San Siro, on a permanent basis, would be a dream and it’s entirely possible that it’s fulfilled. Milan are looking to raise the bar of the squad and whilst maybe not a starter level player, he has the potential to grow substantially.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Glimpses of an impressive player have been seen in recent months, so it’s not an overlookable investment. However, the price must be right, especially with other significant investments planned.

With the recent comments, Calciomercato.com have looked into the loan structure and it’s unfortunately not promising. The loan fee in itself was about €4 million, which isn’t a high cost.

However, to redeem him on a permanent basis, the Rossoneri would be looking at a €50m clause, which is simply unfeasible at this moment. Though it’s worth noting that this figure could potentially be renegotiated.

Right now, it’s unlikely that the Diavolo would take that step, even with a ‘positive season so far’ as the report states. Ruben Amorim believes in him, seeing him as a reliable ally, but more is needed if he’s to achieve his dream.

#2031. West Ham’s Draw Against Lowly Preston – 30 Shots Hide A Far Bigger Problem

Yesterday was a bizarre and surreal experience at the London Stadium as we watched West Ham’s half-hearted attempts to beat a stubborn Preston North End side. Sure, the Hammers had 30 shots and an impressive 79% slice of the possession pie. But scratch below the surface and there are still big problems with Scott Parker’s team, some of which I suspect will not be sorted out until the January transfer window.

Despite West Ham’s impressive array of shots, passes and corners, I never truly felt that the team had the magic or the cutting edge to win the game. And as crazy as it sounds, considering we’d hit the post twice and had 14 corners, I don’t actually think we threatened enough. The Hammers lacked sparkle and magic, for sure.

Alvarez- first game back in claret and blue for a year and a half

Edson Álvarez was an excellent addition to the team, but he is a defensive midfielder, and realistically, the defence was improved. Herrick made a bit of a blooper in goal for the opener, but I felt he redeemed himself with an excellent double save. By and large, West Ham restricted Preston’s chances, and so we should have done. After all, they’re the worst team in the division.

But our biggest problems came in attack. Edvin Austbø on the left wing flattered to deceive, cutting inside and shooting just off target at one point, but never really terrorising his marker, despite the fact that he had him on a yellow card. Joël Piroe did okay but fluffed his big chance when put through by Arne Engels.

As for the supply line, Divine Mukasa flitted in and out of the game and did not create anywhere near enough, given his deployment in the number 10 position. Jarrod Bowen was wide. I mean, very wide for so much of the game that he was probably on first-name terms with the linesman. But realistically, he was just out of the game for large parts of it. We’ll get into more detail on that later.

Overall, it was nowhere near enough quality. Sure, we had momentum. Sure, we had possession. But this did not look like a group of Premier League-standard players against the worst team in the division.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

#2030. Funny ha-ha or funny peculiar? Yesterday had plenty of both

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Here’s a question: did last night’s Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2 match at St James’ Park show we can be the equal of the reigning Premier League champions?

At 16 minutes past six, after a miserably one-sided first half, you would have been embarking on mission impossible to find anyone saying “yes” among the 52,000+plus in the stadium or the millions watching on TV.

By the final whistle, blown nearly 10 minutes after the 90 by Chris Kavanagh, few would have replied “no”. Such is football.

Let’s start at the beginning, or at least on the 12.30 Azuma train from King’s Cross to Newcastle. The LNER service was predictably packed with Gooners. Passengers in Carriage J were overwhelming confident of a one-nil or two-nil to the Arsenal, as they like to crow in north London.

Based on their team’s results this season, that was to be expected. They don’t score many and, apart from a blip near Brighton, they concede even fewer.

Arsenal are, in a word, efficient. I find them boring. The descriptions are not mutually exclusive. No way as the train rumbled into the magnificent Central Station about 32 minutes late was I looking forward to a feast of entertaining football.

In dire need of a drink, I walked up Pink Lane with Big Nige, who had boarded the delayed train at York after it made an unscheduled stop south of the old Viking stronghold of Jorvik. Known as Eboracum in Roman times, btw.

Pink Lane was awash with happy Londoners. There are many, many reasons to be proud of Newcastle; one is the warm welcome the natives offer strangers (excluding Mackems, obviously. There have to be limits).

Which was why the mild hostility that greeted me in the Mosaic Tap was a big surprise. A young chap called Rob walked up to our table, where Paul and Gowa had already got in the drinks, and said: “You can’t wear that scarf in here.”

His mate had apparently clocked me as a Gooner, having mistaken my half-and-half for an Arsenal favour.

A little bit of background. Said scarf was a souvenir from the Bayer Leverkusen v NUFC match. Not that I bought it on my visit to the BayArena shop a mere 11 months ago, when it would have cost £20. This one was acquired in October for a tenner in the NUFC pre-Christmas online sale, while present-buying for my daughter Jo and her family. The PIF need all the help they can get . . .

For all those who detest a half-and-half, that’s your prerogative. I view it as a reminder of a great trip, more useful than a match programme and less likely to be lost.

Rob quickly realised his error, probably because I had slipped into my best am dram persona by screaming: “Look at the scarf! Look at it! You need to go to Specsavers, mate!”

The faux outrage reduced poor Rob to a gibbering, hilariously apologetic wreck. “Sorry, sorry, I’m really sorry. It was my mate . . . What are you drinking, can I get you one, please?”

The free glass of malbec was much appreciated, thanks. Considering the prices at Mosaic, the scarf has probably paid for itself. Funny ha-ha, Rob.

We played the “who would you select” game and all four of us agreed Gonzalez was not justifying his place. Starting Steur was a no-brainer, the back five picked themselves, based on the Fulham game, with Livramento available if needed to give us a second-half lift. The midfield and attack, apart from Steur and Barnes, were as clear as a peasouper.

The big news at 4.15 was Bruno G starting for his new team. Who had expected that?

There was just time for a quick one in Bar Loco, where I bumped into the legendary Tony Mallabar, before safely negotiating Turnstile 31 at the Leazes End. My seat in row MM was in line with the edge of the six-yard box, which gave a perfect view of the fourth goal, unfortunately.

The Booing of Bruno had been a hot topic. My opinion is that every opposition player should be relentlessly jeered, booed, abused and barracked (isn’t SJP on Barrack Road for a reason?) That’s what I recall, perhaps falsely, from big games in the Seventies . . .

Anyway, the Brazilian midfielder was booed from the warm-up until his replacement by Lewis-Skelly when we were leading 2-1. The effort of singling out our former captain probably backfired, because it distracted the more vocal supporters from doing the job of cheering their favourites.

Not that the players or the play gave reasons to be buoyant in the first half. Arsenal did what Arsenal do, using their 11 players against our outfield 10. Whenever Osula or Willock or Murphy or Barnes or Steur attempted to put pressure on Raya, he found the spare man whom our would-be presser had just left unmarked. Boring and efficient by Arsenal. Half-cocked and aimless by the Mags.

In my opinion, Arsenal are no great shakes, whatever the title says. A great team have a top, top striker. They don’t. As they proved by managing only one effort on target before the interval. Hornicek didn’t have a prayer once Hall chested down a long ball and instantly lost possession near the edge of his box.

Our left-back is a wonderful footballer but, having rarely played as a defender in his youth at Chelsea, he is still learning some of the skills essential to be a watertight obstacle.

Murphy tried to catch Raya off his line with a speculative long-range effort and one other shot flew narrowly wide of Raya’s left post via a deflection off Barnes. There was almost nothing else of note in the first half as the champions biffed nearly every shot high, wide and ugly.

Burn and Thiaw stood reasonably firm, Dedic and Murphy seemed on different wavelengths, Steur harried Bruno G and Barnes showed some unlikely aggression. Miley plugged away and Osula ran gamely but United lacked any sort of perceptible gameplan. We rarely managed to find a player in space. Worrying times.

Where was our next goal coming from, wondered my mate Dave at the interval. It had been a while at SJP.

The answer came within four minutes of the restart, soon after the first of three stoppages caused by apparent injuries to Raya. More importantly, after Matthias Jaissle made a triple substitution.

Harvey Barnes smashed a shot low to the keeper’s right, ending a quick attack. Willock had pressured Odegaard into presenting the ball to Osula. An assist on the headless chicken’s credits, fitting reward for another tireless display.

This was when the match became funny peculiar. Miley man-marked Bruno, Arsenal misplaced passes, United won 50:50s, we found space to run with purpose. The gulf in monetary and player resources vanished as the Mags reverted to our best version of Howe-ball.

Only Hornicek of the summer 2026 signings was still on the pitch, Steur having been subbed.

Arsenal looked distinctly second-best. Raya went down again. A corner on our right from Hall was aimed beyond the far post, where the unstoppable Man from Blyth powered a header goalwards. In a frantic kerfuffle, a couple of blocks merely delayed the inevitable. Thiaw smashed it home and we were ahead.

Around me in row MM, the earlier, almost incessant moans and grounds became voices of encouragement. Supporters who had failed to back their team in a dire first half were suddenly full of the joys of November . . .

Ramsey, Livramento and Elanga all caused Arsenal problems. For a few minutes, we battered them.

Then Raya collapsed for a third time. The long delay gave the champions a break they desperately needed.

Whatever anyone else says, Jaissle and his men were right to keep pressing for a third. Arsenal were always going to fashion at least one good chance in the time remaining after we went ahead. To sit back with 28 minutes left, plus a lot of stoppage time, would have been professional suicide.

My suspicion is that those who now bemoan our aggressive play would have whinged even more if the team had sat back. The match became attack and counter-attack. Arsenal, through Madueke doing a decent impression of the absent Saka, kept cutting onto his left foot. Hall, sometimes having to mark two opponents, let the right winger swerve inside and slam a low shot through two defenders and past Hornicek.

The keeper got two hands to the ball but could only push it into the Leazes End net.

Havertz nearly produced what would have been a truly wonderful moment when his head diverted a late Hall corner beyond Kepa and against the crossbar. So near, yet so far.

Then Barnes capped what I reckon was his best game since Wembley 2025 by outstripping Rice on the left touchline and playing the ball perfectly to Ramsey on the edge of the 18-yard box.

In the words of John Ando Anderson, just hit the bloody thing, man. Ramsey did. Sadly, though, instead of putting his laces through it, he tried to bend the ball into the postage stamp and it flew high and wide.

What a feather in Jaissle’s cap a win would have been. One point was good, three would have been great.

The late introduction of Wissa, who replaced Willock, was a failure. He contributed almost nothing, which has been the story all too often since his expensive arrival.

I would have thrown on Fernandez-Pardo as the game opened up. No team enjoy speedy opponents running hard at them and the Belgium international could have been the joker in Jaissle’s pack.

On the balance of play a draw was reasonable but this, like the Liverpool result, felt like two points dropped.

What is inarguable is the team’s willingness to battle for their mates, their manager and the Toon. Long may that continue.

#2029. Why Scott Parker has to resist calls to drop ‘3/10 West Ham Ace’ despite criticism

Taken in isolation yesterday’s team performance at London Stadium doesn’t look quite so poor: A draw against the bottom side who had just beaten promotion prospects Southampton symbolises everything good about this Championship: Predictable it is not.

West Ham hit the wood work four times and on another day could easily have romped home. Trouble is, after the losses and draws of recent weeks a solitary point does nothing to halt the downward slide. It does seem a little early to start demanding change to Parker’s starting eleven – who as a unit were paying together for the first time yesterday.

Nuno was ‘the tinker man’ and you’d hope Scott Parker will persevere, despite criticism and articles today demanding the immediate axing of key players.

Piroe scored on his debut – surely it is a little early to consider discarding the striker who needs a run in Parker’s side

Footballfancast.com is typical in calling for Joel Piroe to be dropped after his poor game:

“The left-footed attacker delivered a dismal display in the centre-forward position and must be dropped by Parker ahead of the trip to Portsmouth in midweek”

The real problem with that knee-jerk reaction is that there is, simply put, nobody else to fill that role: Castellanos was invisible yesterday and fluffed his one chance, a header at the far post that didn’t get within a yard of the target. Pablo is, to all intents and purposes, finished now that his benefactor Nuno has left and until January, the cupboard is bare unless Parker gambles all on one of the youngsters.

Piroe needs the same kind of run which Castellanos had in the team before discarding him: He’s already outscored the Argentine forward by 4 goals to 1 this season. Give him a break.

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

Sad but true Piroe is the only option barring an academy player. Another day we would have won and there were some positives in Alvarez and the young keeper. It’s a long season and in theory we should get better and have a bigger squad than most. Keep the faith – at least it’s easy to like the manager especially with Noble too.

The question is, “Is there anyone else Parker can try, that he hasn’t already?” Piroe may have scored 3 more goals that a player who obviously does not want to play for West Ham, but he has also scored 2 LESS than the CB Mavrapanos. Despite overwhelming advantage in possession and scoring opportunities, Piroe came closer to scoring in his own goal than he did the oppositions yesterday. If anyone is going to be encouraged and given a run in a scoring position, I would prefer it was Ajala than Piroe. As for giving Piroe a chance to show what he can do, he has played in 14 out of the 16 League games so far this season. How much time does he need?

#2028. De Winter discusses importance at Milan, Amorim’s position and the future: “One of us”

Koni De Winter spoke at an event at the AC Milan store today, and he covered numerous topics with a lot of openness.

This season, De Winter has found himself in a new, important light. Matteo Gabbia spent most of pre-season in the middle of the back three, but injuries have prevented him from playing much of a role in the campaign.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It’s an unfortunate shame and there may have been some worries about De Winter taking on this role. However, he’s taken the opportunity in his stride, looking every part a starter in Ruben Amorim’s defence.

Rumours about a new defender arriving will persist, so it’ll be interesting to see what happens with his minutes from January onwards. However, he’s created something of a headache, but it’s a good one to have.

Speaking to SportMediaset on the sidelines of the Meet&Greet at the Milan Store in San Babila, via MilanNews, De Winter looked at the rise in his playing time, Amorim’s closeness to the group and much more.

You also took over at Reggio Emilia when Gabbia was unfortunately injured. You’re practically always there; what does that mean to you?

“I’m playing a lot, it’s great to be playing. We’re playing a lot, and these days you train more on taking care of your body, keeping healthy, and right now I’m doing that more, but it’s great to be playing a lot of games. Playing a lot of games for Milan, and it’s even better to win games.”

It’s all great, but it wasn’t a given: you’ve earned this place as leader. Do you now feel like a leader of this AC Milan?

“I feel good at this Milan club, and as I always say, I try to give what I can. It’s also true that I might have a more important position this year. That might be true, but I always try to do my part, give my all, and help my teammates.”

It’s clear, evident, that Amorim holds you in high regard, but what is Amorim like? An adjective.

“I’d say he’s very human. He’s one of us, he laughs, he has fun, but when he has to be serious, he’s serious. He lives with the group, the group feels close to him, and I think that gives the players a good feeling. It’s nice to work for him and with him.”

Is it true that he got very angry after the defeat against Ferencvaros?

“Yes, but I think the whole group felt that we had played a very poor game, so, as I saw it, my teammates saw it too.”

Are Ferencvaros and Bologna two games you’re ready to say “never again” to? Will Frosinone be a different team?

“Yes, exactly, as I said, we are very confident, but sometimes even too much so, and then all matches are difficult against whoever we play against, and we have to understand this quickly and we can’t make the same mistakes.”

Among the various critics, it’s said that this AC Milan team has enormous potential, but there are too many ups and downs. Does it need more consistency?

“Yes, I think it hurts even more when we lose because we know we can do well, we can win every game. So yes, when we really lose, in the locker room you feel like we’ve let ourselves down first and then everyone else.”

You recently became the father of a beautiful baby girl. What are your nights like as a dad?

“At night, I’m fine. My girlfriend is working really hard, so it’s a lot for me. I mean, I get up sometimes, but it’s much quieter. I think it’s harder for her.”

And how much has life changed with the arrival of a daughter?

“It’s changed a lot, I mean, I don’t know how to explain it. When you’re at work, you think about your daughter, you want to come home earlier, you want to hold her, you want her – I mean, you have more beautiful moments – but it’s hard to explain. I don’t know how to explain it.”

You were also used as a full-back, but now you only play as a centre-back…

“Good, good, because I also consider myself a centre-back, but it’s true that I can also play full-back. It’s something I can do, but it’s not my favourite position. But yes, it’s true that I’ve played a few games there in the past, but I’m happy playing as a centre back and I’m happy that the coach sees that too.”

“I mean, crazy in a good way, yes. He likes to have fun, he likes to dance, he likes to talk, so he’s a bright spot, as they say, for the locker room, yes.”

“Well, that’s a good question. Yes, I miss her. I thought about it even when the little girl was born: I also want to score a goal, I mean, dedicate a goal to her, so I miss her, yes.”

How do you concentrate when you’re in the hotel retreat? How do you focus in the hours leading up to kick-off?

“It’s become a routine now, so I always do the same things. You’re in the hotel, you take a shower, you play a little video game or you’re on your phone, so now I don’t even think about it, it’s really become a routine.”

“He says to stay focused on the game because, as we know, one moment can change the game and at Milan it can also change a season, so it’s very important not to underestimate every moment and always stay focused.

It seems to me that there is a great understanding between you and Strahinja Pavlovic even off the pitch…

“Yes, it’s true, he and I have a good relationship; we met last year. Then when you see him you might not think, I mean, I didn’t think he would be such a great friend, but we got along really well both on and off the pitch, it’s really nice to spend time with him.”

Our 007s at Milanello tell us about some great ping pong matches between you and Pavlovic. Who’s the better player?

“This is difficult, but he started at a much higher level than me. But now I’ve improved a lot, although I have to say he’s even stronger. But yes, every day we start with a game of ping pong and then we start working.”

Would you like your daughter to play soccer in the future? Are you planning a second child? Would you like to have a son who plays soccer?

“I want her to do what she wants, where she feels good, where she doesn’t feel pressured, and where she can express herself best. And then, going back to ping pong, I think there’s some video; maybe we can see me beat her.”

#2026. West Ham’s Answer Was There All Along – So Why Ignore It?

West Ham United’s lack of cutting edge against Preston North End was concerning, but perhaps the most frustrating aspect of Saturday’s 1-1 draw was that Scott Parker already appears to have the answer to the Hammers’ creative problems.

At the risk of sounding like a scratched record, West Ham have an emergency, break-glass solution to breaking teams down. It’s called Jarrod Bowen, and I’m not entirely sure I’ve ever seen our captain play wider than he did at the London Stadium yesterday.

What’s particularly puzzling is that I genuinely believe the best we’ve seen Bowen play in the last couple of years came during the second half against Cardiff City. On that occasion, Parker was effectively handed a blueprint for getting the best out of West Ham’s most important player, yet we’ve barely seen it since.

During that extraordinary second-half comeback against Cardiff, Bowen was given a certain amount of freedom, perhaps encouraged by Parker or maybe he just took it upon himself to drift into the middle of the pitch and cause havoc.

Whatever the reason, he had a hand in all three West Ham goals, and the difference was remarkable.

For the first, he drifted into what might be regarded as the number 10 position and chipped a lovely ball over the Cardiff back line for Divine Mukasa to finish.

The second was similar, with Bowen again creating the opening from a central position. His pass found Joël Piroe, whose flick released Arne Engels to score.

The third goal saw Bowen back in his more familiar position on the right-hand side, where he supplied a wonderful inswinging cross for Max Kilman to equalise.

Jarrod Bowen was given license to roam against Cardiff

But that only went to show quite how much freedom Bowen had. In essence, he was everywhere.

As a blueprint, Scott Parker couldn’t have been given a better gift on his first day in charge than discovering that West Ham’s best player could operate with devastating effect from a free role.

Indeed, I was so encouraged by what I saw that I subsequently wrote about how Scott Parker must restore West Ham’s most dangerous weapon following the defeat at Blackburn.

Because for a brief period against Cardiff, it looked as though we’d stumbled upon something rather special.

Therefore, I was a little underwhelmed that we didn’t see it repeated against Blackburn and very worried when we probably saw our captain more straightjacketed than ever against Preston North End.

If I could offer Parker one piece of encouragement or advice, it would be to get the best out of Bowen.

I’m quite sure our new head coach will improve the defence, and I think we saw signs of that yesterday, albeit against the league’s worst team.

But it can’t come at the expense of shackling our best player, who potentially could only be here for a few more months.

As I argued in my assessment of the Preston draw, West Ham had plenty of possession, shots and territory, but very little magic.

And that’s the really bloody annoying part. We have a player who can provide exactly that, but we’re asking him to operate in a way which makes life considerably easier for the opposition.

I know one thing. If I was head coach of an opposition Championship team and I saw Jarrod Bowen shackled to the right wing, I’d breathe a huge sigh of relief.

If we don’t succeed in getting promotion, Bowen could leave for a pittance of £15m. That’s the release clause in the revised contract he agreed following relegation.

We do know that Bowen flew to Prague to meet Daniel Křetínský before pledging to remain at West Ham for another season, as he explained in his interview with Sky Sports.

And I’m now very fearful that we are going to waste what should really be something of a cheat code for the division.

Bowen is comfortably our best attacking player, and we’ve already seen how devastating he can be when allowed to roam. Yet rather than building upon that discovery, Parker appears to have returned him to a position where he’s easier to mark and less able to influence the game.

I wish it weren’t so, but I’ve now come to the conclusion that the second half against Cardiff was a pure accident rather than a window into what we could begin to see from Scott Parker as he got his teeth into the West Ham job.

But decisions like that could well make the difference between automatic promotion and a play-off place, if we’re lucky.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

#2025. “Superb” – Parker’s delight over reversing Nuno’s biggest mistake | West Ham News

24 hours on from West Ham’s  tepid point against the bottom side in the league and whilst the justified criticism is flying around, there are definitely positives to pull out of a fixture in which West Ham dominated all the important statistics save the most important one: The points tally at the final whistle.

Sadly, again the Hammers have lost ground on the leaders and now sit eight points adrift. And yet, from Scott Parker’s comments, there are definite signs that he’s learned from at least some of the mistakes made by his predecessor. Reversing Nuno’s decision to cast out Edson Alvarez from the senior team proved a massive success.. Who knew.

Yesterday’s re-integration of ‘El Machin’ into the starting line up was his first league appearance in a West Ham shirt since May 2025.

As Scott Parker summed up, Alvarez did not let him down:

“He brought every bit of what we needed. It’s a young team, and his experience today in terms of organising and his general presence on the pitch was very, very good for us for large aspects.

“It was a big ask and I knew that going into the game, he hasn’t played at all this year and probably hasn’t had a lot of training in and around the first team. But I just felt his experience and know-how around it was needed, and for sure he was a massive part today of why we performed the way we performed” (Justin Allen- YouTube)

The Mexican clearly cares: He was in tears before kick off, so tough has his time in the football wilderness been.

If he can maintain that kind of focus and form, Parker may well have found the missing piece in West Ham’s defensive jigsaw puzzle, that proved beyond his predecessor who simply wouldn’t extend the olive branch to any of his ‘frozen out’ players.

#2023. West Ham’s home problem summed up in one sentence – by a Preston fan

Preston North End, the bottom side in the Championship, arrived in east London yesterday unaffected by the occasion and kept West Ham at bay for an hour until Dinos Mavropanos headed equaliser restored parity and saved Scott Parker’s blushes.

Two weeks’ work during the international break had accounted for very little as Preston withstood everything the Hammers and their almost 60,000 fans had to throw at their lowly opponents.

And therein lies the problem. Having surrendered the small, intimidating, sometimes downright hostile atmosphere of Upton Park back in 2016, the distance from the pitch and the wide open spaces of the Olympic Stadium are about as intimidating as a day out at London Zoo for our opponents and their fans who continue to pour scorn on the venue.

It just doesn’t strike fear into opponents as it should. Even when we score.

Isolated tiers in the stadium and poor pitch proximity do little to help the atmosphere at the London Stadium – as our opponents are finding out

Preston fan Tm Mercer, writing in the Lancashire Evening Post, makes it abundantly clear that there was no noticeable crowd reaction to lift the home side, as there should have been once Mavropanos restored parity:

“Aside from play-off finals, I’m pretty certain it is the first time I’ve been in a stadium for a league match with 60,000-plus through the gate.

Yet, when they equalised, it did not feel like the roar of that many people in such a cavernous ground. Give me somewhere like Gigg Lane, stood in their paddock pitch side, any day!”

For the uninitiated, Gigg Lane is the home of Bury FC with a capacity of around…..12,000.

Nobody is suggesting the Hammers fans were silent. The cursèd accoustics from the soulless bowl and sheer distance from the pitch play right into opponents’ hands.  And, ten years after moving in, it’s going to take a lot more than some safe standing and a couple of family zones to fix it.

A sterner test will come at Portsmouth but saving Koppen’s transfer budget for the acquisition of a striker who can actually hit the target looks to be the 100% absolute stone-cold priority in January, if it isn’t already too late.

And Herrick’s emergence has probably boosted the funds available to Koppen significantly.

Rangers will be holding talks behind the scenes over the possibility of a move to secure further investment in the coming years.

The American owners are looking to sell a small percentage of the Premier League outfit, in order to bring in fresh money to help develop the club on and off the pitch.

Wyness believes that Rangers could explore a similar move within the next few years, but still have plenty of improvements to make before they reach that stage.

The disparity between the two clubs is significant at the moment, even though Wyness believes that the 49ers’ plans are beginning to work at Ibrox.

He feels that if the Gers can continue to progress on their current trajectory, then the prospect of similar investment is not out of the question in future.

Aberdeen’s former chief Wyness – who served as CEO at Pittodrie between 2000 and 2004 and now runs a consultancy business advising elite clubs – believes that Rangers fans shouldn’t be concerned over the 49ers’ ability to fund both clubs long-term.

The Scottish businessman sees their push for a new investment as a move to help realise their ambitions, rather than an indication that they are struggling to help the clubs progress.

Speaking on the latest edition of Football Insider’s Inside Track podcast, he explained how “conversations” are likely already taking place for Rangers to get a similar financial boost.

“Look, the fact is Rangers are not as attractive as Leeds in terms of the revenue situation and the profit going forward. But Rangers are showing signs of turning things around a little bit as a financial model,” he said.

“Now, I think Rangers should be very happy having the 49ers still as owners there. And I think they're making progress.

“I think they’ll be the conversations that are going on. They're starting to show signs of doing things correctly and getting the right structure together. So no, I wouldn't be concerned in the slightest if I was a Rangers fan. I think it's just good, prudent management from the 49ers.”

#2015. Roy Keane savages Man United players and fellow Sky pundit in brutal post-match verdict

Senior Correspondent AUTHORITY Senior football correspondent and podcast host with specialist knowledge across the Premier League and SPFL. FOCUS Transfer news, breaking stories, and behind-the-scenes insight across Arsenal, Liverpool, Celtic, and Manchester United. THE INSIGHT Callum utilises a network of club and industry contacts across the Premier League and SPFL to deliver verified, high-speed reporting. He provides the depth behind the headlines — from breaking transfer news to behind-the-scenes developments — ensuring fans get the full story as it happens.

Roy Keane was left furious following Manchester United's heavy defeat against Liverpool and made his anger very clear.

The former Red Devils midfielder, and no-nonsense pundit, savaged the current crop of players as well as his fellow pundit Gary Neville in the wake of the 4-0 defeat.

Mauricio Pochettino's side fell 2-0 down just 13 minutes into the game, after Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz found the net following an early red card for Leny Yoro.

Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz doubled the scoreline in the second half, and Liverpool could have had more, having created countless chances to put their rivals away.

There were echoes of the 7-0 win Liverpool recorded against Man United in 2023, and yet, the fans applauded the players off the pitch and pundits have begun making excuses.

Keane, however, was not in a mood to tolerate excuses and he demanded the players take responsibility and the pundits, including Gary Neville, assess their priorities.

Yoro's red card is largely being pinned as the reason for Man United's defeat, having ripped up any plans they had heading into what was always set to be a tough game.

However, Keane has insisted that cannot be the only reason for the defeat, as he questioned how teams have coped in the past after going down to ten men early in the game.

While the 4-0 scoreline did flatter Man United, that should be treated as a major concern rather than a positive to take from the game, and Keane has made his feelings clear.

Speaking live on Sky Sports, he ranted: "If I hear that one more time from the lads on commentary and in the studio, '4-0 is not too bad, we were down to ten men', has a team never got a result before with ten men?

"I thought they were so bad. Neville, who's played for Man United hundreds of times, saying he's okay with 4-0? Are you telling me they couldn't have done better?

"At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality. I can't believe what I'm hearing from people who've played for the club.

"The fans are applauding the players. Applauding what? Applauding rubbish.

"This team, two years ago, finished 15th and the last year or two we're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers, when do the players take responsibility?

"Liverpool probably should've scored eight or nine, and everyone's coming off the pitch saying 'four's not too bad', I feel like swearing."

Despite the result and Keane's rant, there can be no doubt that the biggest talking point will centre around Yoro's red card and the impact it had on the game.

While it should not be used as an excuse for their dismal performance, it certainly weakened the side, and Liverpool took full advantage in the minutes that followed.

However, former PGMOL chief Keith Hackett told Football Insider that Man United may have reason to complain after analysing footage of Yoro's dismissal.

While referee Sam Barrott made a quick decision to brandish a red card for denying a goalscoring opportunity, replays suggested it may not have met all of the criteria.

Questions have been asked about whether Alexander Isak would have got to the ball, and as a result, the subjective decision is bound to cause debates.
